books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

stimulus.text: Described: a pair of statistical maps from the United States Census Office (1898) showing where Irish-born residents lived in 1890. The darkest shading, marking the heaviest concentrations of Irish-born residents relative to population, falls over the industrial Northeast and the Great Lakes port cities, with far lighter shading across the rural South and the far West.
stimulus.source_note: Described from the Census Office maps, Density of Distribution of the Natives of Ireland: 1890, Government release of 11th Census Results, 1898. Public domain. Rewrite of staged survivor pr25e-test2-q36 (Princeton Practice Test 2), reframed to Gilded Age restriction measures; stem, options, and explanations are original.

stem: A nativist in 1890 looking at these maps would most likely have argued that

options.text: immigration had already ended on its own by 1890
options.misconception: Claims the maps show an ending, but they show people living here.

options.text: the Irish had spread too thinly to affect American life
options.misconception: Reads clustering as spreading thin, the opposite of the shading.

options.text: new immigrants should be welcomed into the South and West
options.misconception: Gives the nativist a welcoming position nativists did not hold.

options.text: immigrants were concentrating in cities instead of spreading out as Americans

rationales.A: The maps show Irish-born residents living in American cities in 1890. Nothing here shows immigration ending.
rationales.B: The shading shows clustering, not thin spreading. The Irish were concentrated, not scattered.
rationales.C: Welcoming immigrants into new regions was the opposite of the nativist position. Nativists wanted restriction, not resettlement.
rationales.D: The maps show Irish-born residents concentrated in the industrial Northeast and Great Lakes port cities. Background from the books: a nativist would read that clustering as proof that immigrants stayed apart in city enclaves instead of spreading out and becoming American.
rationales.general:
Put yourself in the nativist's place and read the map as the nativist would.
1. The darkest shading falls over the industrial Northeast and the Great Lakes port cities.
2. That means Irish-born residents clustered in cities, not across the country.
3. Background from the books: nativists feared that new immigrants stayed apart and weakened American identity.
4. So the nativist would point to the clustering as the problem itself.
Remember: a point of view question asks how the person in the stem would read the evidence.
